The wealth of nations has been a shared obsession among economists, sociologists, philosophers, and political theorists throughout history. But historical evidence and empirical data tell us the relationship isn't nearly that straightforward—in fact, it's often misleading.

articles.author: Abubakar
articles.description:
Context


A Kong gateway plugin was implemented to reject API requests violating a contract rule (len(values) ≤ n) before they reach upstream services. Enforcement is placed at the gateway layer, preventing invalid requests from entering downstream execution paths.
In distributed systems, enforcement can occur at multiple layers. The critical distinction is whether enforcement prevents execution or reports failure after the fact.
A control layer is one where invalid actions are stopped before execution. This differs from validation layers, which detect violations after the action has been attempted and report the failure.
The invariant: Enforcement placed after execution is reporting, not control.
"May this action proceed?"
"Was this action invalid?"
These questions are not interchangeable…
articles.title: Authority Placement: Control Layers and Enforcement Boundaries

I used to believe good backend engineering meant preparing for the future from day one.
Clean architecture.
Perfect boundaries.
Systems that could scale before they ever needed to.
It felt responsible. It felt professional. What I didn’t understand yet was this: early-stage systems rarely fail because of load. They fail because they become hard to change.
I learned this while working on a backend that looked excellent on paper. We had separate modules, clear interfaces, and well-defined responsibilities. Authentication lived in its own area. Messaging had its own flow. Even internal calls were abstracted behind contracts.
The architecture diagram was beautiful. The product, however, moved slowly.
A small feature request like "add one field to the response" meant touching multiple layers, u…

articles.author: OscarMarulanda
articles.description:
Hey, would you mind taking a look at my app and telling me what you think? I'd really appreciate it. nicehaus.fooorms.com (fooorms.com is another app I made).
My gf and I are living together since july last year, and have been splitting expenses equally. So we keep a google sheets document where we enter everything each one of us pays for, and if one is lagging behind, that person has to pay for the next few things to catch up.
But I don't like manually writing the entries, and sometimes I put it off so long that I forget some expenses :'v Same thing happens to her, although not as often.
So I created NiceHaus (Haus because she teaches German) to be able to enter expenses through voice prompts, and also shopping list items, and to-do list items. You say, "I bought eggs for 3 dollars, Lucía bought some sheets for 20, and we have to paint the kitchen wall", the app records you, Anthropic's Haiku 4.5 parses the transcription into manageable json, it gets saved, and the frontend organizes and shows it.
So yeah, I'd appreciate your comments and suggestions :)
articles.title: NiceHaus, a household-managing AI-powered web app

Alfred Wahlforss was running out of options. His startup, Listen Labs, needed to hire over 100 engineers, but competing against Mark Zuckerberg's $100 million offers seemed impossible. So he spent $5,000 — a fifth of his marketing budget — on a billboard in San Francisco displaying what looked like gibberish: five strings of random numbers.
The numbers were actually AI tokens. Decoded, they led to a coding challenge: build an algorithm to act as a digital bouncer at Berghain, the Berlin nightclub famous for rejecting nearly everyone at the door. Within days, thousands attempted the puzzle. 430 cracked it. Some got hired. The winner flew to Berlin, all expenses paid.
